Audit which receivers listened on which days

Source: R/audit_listening.R
audit_listening.Rd

Builds one row per receiver serial and UTC date on which a deployment had the receiver in the water, and decides whether the receiver was listening. A missing detection is evidence of absence only on a day the receiver was listening, so a positioning or residency analysis reads this table instead of the deployment dates alone. The table is keyed by the receiver serial: a receiver swap leaves two receivers at one station on one day, each with its own row.

Usage

audit_listening(
  x,
  reference_tags = NULL,
  min_share = 0.5,
  max_silent_days = NULL,
  known_listening = NULL,
  logs = NULL
)

Arguments

x

A detset().

reference_tags

Optional data frame with transmitter, and optionally receiver_serial to name the receivers expected to hear each. When it is NULL and the deployments carry receiver_transmitter (see read_deployments()), those ids are the reference tags, with a message, and with no receiver_serial: a receiver is expected to hear one when it heard it on min_share of its full days, so a receiver that never logs its own built-in transmitter is not held to it. An id the animals table also lists is left out with a warning.

min_share

Share of full days, from 0 to 1, a receiver must hear a reference tag to be expected to hear it every day, when reference_tags has no receiver_serial.

max_silent_days

Optional length, in days, of a run of silent days that marks the receiver as not listening for the whole run. No default: without it only a receiver silent on every day is "silent_run".

known_listening

Optional receivers known to have worked: a character vector of receiver serials, or a data frame with receiver_serial and, optionally, date for receiver-days. Their "silent_run" days become "silent", which is listening.

logs

Optional receiver logs, from read_receiver_logs().

Value

x with listening replaced by the audit and one log record. The table has receiver_serial (NA for a deployment with no serial), station_id, date, deployed_share, detections (all transmitters), reference_detections (NA where no reference tag is expected), status and listening (logical). With logs it also has log_records, the status records of the day (NA

outside the receiver's log), and pings, the pulses its DIAG records counted (NA without them), before status. The table's attribute data_end holds each deployment's data end as the audit set it (receiver_serial, station_id, deploy_datetime, data_end), and as_detfield_input() reads these ends.

Details

A deployment with no receiver_serial, as in OTN's deployment CSV and stations-receivers file, is keyed by its station_id instead. Its rows keep receiver_serial as NA, and a detection at that station counts for them unless its receiver has a deployment of its own. This is the rule detfield::bin_detections() uses for such rows.

Each receiver-day gets one status:

  • "not_downloaded": a day that starts at or after the end of the receiver's data, so its data are not in the set. The data end at the recorded download (download_datetime) when it comes before the recovery. Not listening, also on a day with detections after the download (see below).

  • "silent_run": a day of a receiver at a station that logged no detection of any transmitter over all its days in the table (a day or more in the water), or, when max_silent_days is given, a day in a run of at least that many consecutive silent days. Not listening: a receiver that hears nothing while the array logs detections is more likely dead than alone.

  • "partial": a day the receiver's data cover in part: a deployment or recovery day, or the day of a download that comes before the recovery. deployed_share gives the share of the day in the water, so it is 1 on such a download day. Listening; as_detfield_input() ends the deployment at the download, so the hours after it are not used.

  • "reference_silent": a full day with no detection of any transmitter, on which the receiver was expected to hear at least one reference tag. Not listening.

  • "reference_missed": a full day on which the receiver heard none of the reference tags it is expected to hear but logged other detections. Kept as listening, because a receiver that logs detections was working; the reference tag may have been out of range that day.

  • "silent": a full day with no detection of any transmitter and no reference tag to say whether the receiver worked. Kept as listening, because a quiet day can be a day with no animal near; check these days.

  • "listening": every other day.

Receiver logs. With logs, from read_receiver_logs(), the audit also reads the receiver's own status records (DIAG, TEMP, ATTITUDE, BATTERY and HEALTH, hourly on a VR2Tx), on the full days, before the download, on which the receiver logged no detection. A receiver's log covers the UTC dates from its first to its last record, events included, in each file; the receiver's EVENT_OFFLOAD record, written at download, closes the span. On such a day inside the span:

  • "off": no status record at all. The receiver was not running, as after a power failure or a flat battery. Not listening.

  • "deaf": status records, and a reference tag expected and not heard (the day would otherwise be "reference_silent"). The receiver ran and decoded nothing, the reference tag included. Not listening. The pings column shows whether its hydrophone counted pulses that day: if it did, noise or a reference tag out of range are more likely than a dead hydrophone.

  • "logging_silent": status records and no reference tag expected (the day would otherwise be "silent"). The receiver ran and heard nothing. Kept as listening, as a silent day is.

  • "listening": status records whose log_detections count detections. A receiver counts every transmitter it decodes, whatever project the tag belongs to and whether or not the detection is in the set, so the receiver heard that day. A day that would otherwise be "reference_silent" or "deaf" becomes "reference_missed": the receiver heard something, though not the reference tag. A DIAG record counts the detections since the receiver's previous DIAG record, so a count is given to a day only when that interval lies inside the day: the record at midnight, the first record of a file and the first after a gap across midnight are left out. The log record counts these days.

When the evidence disagrees: a detection in the set beats the log, so a day with a detection keeps its status, and a day with detections and no status record inside the span is counted in the log record. A logged count beats the rules that make a quiet day not listening: the day is listening, and a receiver whose log counted detections on any day did not hear nothing on all its days, so the first "silent_run" rule above does not apply to it. "off" beats "silent_run", and no count can lift an "off" day: counts are read from status records only, so a day with a count has a status record. A run of "logging_silent" days still becomes "silent_run" under the run rules below, because a log shows that a receiver ran and cannot show that it heard; known_listening turns those days back to "logging_silent". Days outside every span of their receiver, and every day of a receiver with no log, get the statuses above, as without logs. logs may also be a table of your own with receiver_serial, datetime (UTC) and record_type; a record type other than EVENT, EVENT_FAULT, EVENT_INIT and EVENT_OFFLOAD counts as a status record.

The audit reads every transmitter in the set. Cut to one species, it marks as silent the receivers that heard only other species; run it on every transmitter the receivers logged, reference tags included, and cut with filter_animals() after it.

Where evidence of listening is lost. A detection removed before the audit is no longer evidence that the receiver heard. Three steps remove them: an export that holds one project's tags (below); filter_animals() run before the audit; and the filters of false and unwanted detections, filter_min_lag(), filter_post_release() and filter_duplicates(), whose removed detections were still decoded by a working receiver. On the example, run after those three filters, the audit gives 8 of 180 receiver-days "silent" that it gives "listening" when run before them, as vignette("detqc") runs it. A receiver's log counts every detection it decoded, so logs recover such days, and the evidence an export never held.

A GLATOS or OTN detection export is cut in the same way before it reaches you: it holds one project's tags only. A partner receiver that worked but heard none of them, or heard none for max_silent_days, reads as "silent_run". In a GLATOS export, a partner receiver that logged detections in a month can still read as "silent_run" for many of that month's receiver-days, because none of its detections were of the export's tags. The audit warns with these counts when any day is "silent_run" and the set looks cut: its detections come from such an export, filter_animals() ran before the audit, or the detections hold fewer species than the animals table lists. The log record names the reasons, and processing_report() repeats them beside the count. known_listening names the receivers known to have worked, such as those in the network's receiver file with data, so their silent days stay "silent" and listening.

A receiver is expected to hear a reference tag when reference_tags pairs them by receiver_serial. Without that column, a receiver is expected to hear a tag when it heard it on at least min_share of its full days within the tag's span, from the tag's first to its last detection by any receiver. Days outside that span are not tested against that tag.

A deployment still in the water listens until its download, or, with no download time, until the last detection in the set. A deployment with no recovery time ends where the same receiver (by receiver_serial) is deployed again.

Detections after the download. A deployment's data end at its recorded download, whatever the detections say. A detection after that download and before the deployment ends stays in the set. Its day stays "not_downloaded", which is not listening, and the detection is counted in detections. Such a detection can mean a download time recorded too early, a later download missing from the sheet, a receiver that kept logging after the download, or a clock that was wrong. detset() marks these detections in the column after_download, and the check detections_after_download of check_detset() lists them by deployment. A detection the receiver logged at its next deployment belongs to that deployment. A message counts these detections, their deployments and the "not_downloaded" receiver-days that hold them, and the log record repeats the counts. Where the sheet is wrong, correct the download time and build the set again; where the detections are false, remove them before the audit. The table covers the UTC dates from the first to the last detection in the set: outside them the set holds no data to audit, as when it was cut to one month.

Examples

study <- detqc_example
dets <- detset(study$detections, study$deployments, study$animals)
dets <- audit_listening(dets, known_listening = unique(dets$deployments$receiver_serial))
table(dets$listening$status)
#> 
#> listening    silent 
#>        77       103 
# With the receivers' own logs
log_files <- list.files(system.file("extdata", "receiver_logs", package = "detqc"),
                        full.names = TRUE)
logs <- read_receiver_logs(log_files)
dets <- audit_listening(dets, known_listening = unique(dets$deployments$receiver_serial),
                        logs = logs)
table(dets$listening$status)
#> 
#>      listening logging_silent            off         silent 
#>             77             92              2              9
